title: The prisoner's dilemma
examples: What does the prisoner's dilemma actually show about people?
Is it always best to be selfish in this situation?
How can we make people cooperate when it is easier to cheat?

explain.say: Today we explore a puzzle called the prisoner's dilemma. It looks at choices between working together or acting alone. We will see how self-interest affects cooperation.

items: Acting alone seems safer in the short term.

explain.say: The dilemma shows a conflict between what is best for the group. Sometimes, individual gain hurts the whole group. Think about sharing a scarce resource.
Game theory is the study of strategic decision-making. It helps us predict choices when people interact. It models how rational people think about each other.

items: Predicting the outcome is the goal

explain.say: Consider two students deciding on a group project. They can either both study hard or one can slack off. If one slacks, the other does better.
In real life, think about traffic rules. If everyone follows the rules, the journey is smooth. If a few ignore them, everyone slows down.
A common mistake is assuming people always think about the long term. Sometimes, immediate rewards override future group happiness. This is the core tension.

items: Focusing only on the next turn

faq.q: Why do both prisoners confess in the dilemma?
faq.a: Both confess because confessing is the best individual choice, even if it leads to a worse outcome for both together. This is the core conflict.
asks: Why is confessing the dominant strategy?

faq.q: Is cooperation always better than self-interest?
faq.a: Not necessarily. While cooperation is ideal, the dilemma shows that self-interest can sometimes force a suboptimal outcome for everyone.
asks: Can we trust people to cooperate?

faq.q: What is game theory really used for?
faq.a: It models strategic interactions in many fields. It helps predict outcomes when multiple rational actors are involved, like in economics or politics.
asks: Is game theory just for games?
What are the limits of game theory?

faq.a: It is a state where no player can improve their outcome by unilaterally changing their strategy, assuming others keep theirs the same. It is a stable point.
asks: What is a stable point in this game?
Does the Nash Equilibrium mean cooperation?

faq.q: Does the dilemma prove that cooperation is impossible?
faq.a: No. It shows that cooperation is difficult to maintain without some form of external agreement or repeated interaction. Trust is key.
asks: Is there a way around this dilemma?

facts: The Prisoner's Dilemma models a conflict between individual incentives and collective welfare.
Game theory analyzes strategic decision-making among rational agents.
The Nash Equilibrium describes a stable outcome where no player benefits from changing alone.
Repeated interactions can encourage cooperation by introducing the threat of future punishment.

quiz.say: If both players cooperate, the outcome is:
quiz.why: When both cooperate, they achieve the best possible outcome for the group.

wrong.0: This is the outcome if both players defect.
wrong.1: This is the outcome if only one player defects.
wrong.2: This suggests an outcome not defined in the standard setup.

quiz.say: In game theory, what does a 'rational' player assume?

options.show: They choose the best option for themselves.
options.say: They choose the best option for themselves.

options.show: They always choose the cooperative option.
options.say: They always choose the cooperative option.

options.show: They only consider the group's needs.
options.say: They only consider the group's needs.

quiz.why: Rationality in this context means acting to maximize one's own payoff, regardless of others.

wrong.1: This ignores the possibility of self-interest leading to defection.
wrong.2: This overlooks the individual incentive to gain more.
wrong.3: While they consider others, the model focuses on calculated outcomes, not emotion.

quiz.say: If cooperation is repeated many times, what often increases?
quiz.why: Knowing you will interact again makes cheating riskier, encouraging better long-term behavior.

wrong.0: Repetition usually simplifies the strategy towards mutual trust.
wrong.2: While temptation exists, the fear of future retaliation usually lowers it.
wrong.3: The immediate payoff is what the dilemma highlights, not the long-term trend.
